title: UNH officials say rise in reported rape cases could show more survivors are coming forward - WMUR
content: The new investigation of an alleged rape at Cornell University is drawing attention to college campuses across the country and how they handle assault allegations. The recent Security and Fire Safety Report at the University of New Hampshire shows that reported rape cases are up on and off campus, but the school and advocates argue that could show their efforts to connect victims to resources are working. "As a woman myself, it's terrifying to think about," said UNH sophomore Tess Vallas. Students at UNH said the reports coming out of Cornell University are hard to hear. >> Download the free WMUR app to get updates on the go << "Honestly, it's just really disappointing," said UNH freshman Madeline Dowling. They said it's also hard to hear that their school is reporting a rise in rape cases in the past three years. There were 26 cases reported in 2023, 41 in 2024 and 46 in 2025. "I don't see why that wouldn't be a concern for anyone," Vallas said. "It's not good," said UNH sophomore Tristan White. "It doesn't help either party in the end." UNH said it takes such crimes very seriously and has increased its training to make sure victims have the best support available. School officials said they believe those efforts are why the rape case reports are rising, because more survivors feel comfortable coming forward and not necessarily because more crimes are occurring. UNH offers resources through its SHARPP Center for Interpersonal Violence Awareness, Prevention and Advocacy on campus and partners with the state's Coalition Against Domestic and Sexual Violence to help victims navigate what follows after making a report. "An advocate can help walk a survivor through what each of those are going to look like and what their options are," said Emily Provencher, prevention and child welfare specialist. Those services are available 24/7 and offer a confidential advocate who helps survivors explore their next steps, such as filing a criminal or Title IX complaint or doing nothing at all. Provencher said they're trained to offer the support a survivor needs. "They're going to center everything on what you want and what works best for you," she said. The coalition said that after reports like the Cornell investigation come out, it sees an increase in calls to the center from survivors who feel they can step up after seeing other survivors come forward. If you or someone you know is a victim of sexual abuse, you can call the state's 24/7 sexual assault hotline at 866-644-3574 to be connected with resources. title: UNH Dunkin' Mural: Artist Hides Self-Portrait at MUBkin - Hoodline
content: A massive new mural now stretches across the Dunkin' inside the University of New Hampshire's Memorial Union Building, and if you look closely enough, you might spot the artist herself tucked into the scene wearing a cap and gown. Madeline Pender, a UNH alumna, was hired by Dunkin' to envision and paint the artwork as part of a redesign that turns the beloved campus coffee shop into the chain's first college-campus Signature Series store in New England. Pender painted the mural, which spans the length of the Dunkin' store. She included a self-portrait tucked into the scene. The mural, unveiled Thursday at the Dunkin' location inside the Memorial Union Building, features UNH student athletes, Thomson Hall, the Wildcat statue, and students clutching coffee and donuts, per the same account. It's a fitting tribute for a space students have long called their own. The Memorial Union Building's Dunkin' is so central to daily life on campus that students have nicknamed it “MUBkin,” according to the University of New Hampshire. The store is a familiar campus fixture, and Dunkin' chose it for its signature redesign. Pender also depicted Eli Bryant, a 2024 UNH alumnus and one of her closest friends, standing at an easel inside the mural, according to the Globe's reporting. The artwork he's shown painting on his easel depicts a waterfaring vessel built by UNH students. DriX is an autonomous surface vessel; UNH's Center for Coastal and Ocean Mapping has housed and supported DriX vessels since December 2018, according to UNH's Center for Coastal and Ocean Mapping. The campus landmarks woven throughout the mural carry their own histories. Thomson Hall, one of the primary buildings rendered in the artwork, is a Romanesque structure at the center of campus listed on the National Register of Historic Places, according to Society19. The Wildcat statue is another campus icon featured in the mural. The Memorial Union Building is the setting for the mural. Pender worked with Dunkin' and UNH representatives through several mural iterations before the final design came together, the Globe reports. She hand-painted the design elements herself, and the artwork was then assembled as a digital collage and printed onto the wall covering. The project marks the first Dunkin' Signature Series store on a college campus in New England, per Dunkin'. Pender said senior year was the first time campus life started to feel normal again, the Globe reports, a detail that adds personal weight to her return to UNH as both teacher and muralist. Her mural leaves a lasting imprint at UNH. Pender's mural brings new artwork to the Memorial Union Building. The MUBkin is now home to Dunkin's Signature Series store and Pender's mural. The sprawling mural gives the campus coffee shop a distinctive new look, with a UNH alumna's own face now watching over the counter. title: NH’s public colleges will waive tuition for eligible students - New Hampshire Public Radio
content: Beginning next year, certain students will get free tuition at New Hampshire's state colleges. To be eligible, students must be New Hampshire residents, meet certain academic requirements and be attending one of the schools for the first time. Their families cannot earn more than $100,000 a year. The University System of New Hampshire announced the program, The New Hampshire Promise, Thursday. In a statement, Gov. Kelly Ayotte said tuition waivers will be good for students and employers. “By expanding affordable pathways to higher education, we’re creating more opportunities for our young people to pursue good-paying jobs and making it easier for them to build their careers in New Hampshire,” she said. Under a prior version of the program, which was tied to federal loan eligibility requirements, nearly 4,000 students received tuition waivers between 2017 and this academic year. Tania deLuzuriaga, a University of New Hampshire spokesperson, said they estimate the change in eligibility requirements will mean an additional 29% of next year’s incoming class will qualify for the program. Under the prior program, students had to complete a lengthy and complicated federal Pell Grant application before they knew whether they would qualify for federal aid. That can be a hurdle, deLuzuriaga said, especially for first-generation students whose family members have not navigated the process before. Now, students know up front whether they qualify and only need to fill out the standard federal financial aid application. New Hampshire's public colleges and universities lost nearly $20 million in the last state budget. That prompted UNH to cut $17.5 million from its budget, leading to staff cuts and a hiring freeze. Student enrollment has also been declining. Kimberly DeRego, chief enrollment officer for the University System of New Hampshire, said in an email that the schools will pay for the tuition waivers with money from its endowment. The University System also hopes the new program will attract donors who want to support lower-income students. Students can enroll at UNH, Plymouth State University, Keene State College and UNH’s College of Professional Studies online program, and do not have to live on campus. They must have earned at least a 2.7 GPA at their prior school and be a full-time student. The waivers could save students between $12,000 and $16,000 a year in tuition, depending on where they enroll. Tuition for UNH’s College of Professional Studies costs about $7,700 a year. Students will still have to pay for room and board and fees. The tuition waiver is available only to first-year students and transfer students who have earned an associate's degree at one of the state’s community colleges. It is not open to current students unless they are receiving tuition waivers under the prior program. Students will continue receiving tuition waivers throughout their college degree as long as they continue to meet the eligibility requirements. Students do not have to apply to be considered. The University System will use information from the federal student loan application to determine if they are eligible. Saint Anselm College in Manchester began its own tuition waiver program last year for New Hampshire and Maine students. Last month, it announced it was explaining eligibility to Vermont students. title: UNH Stock Tracks Hot Monthly Streak: Wall Street Cheers ‘Impressive’ Q2 And Sees Over 20% More Room To Run - Stocktwits
content: Shares of UnitedHealth Group, Inc. (UNH) are headed for their fourth monthly win as Wall Street turns more bullish after a large second-quarter (Q2) earnings beat and a sweeping increase to its 2026 outlook. UNH stock rose 1% on Friday, bringing its monthly gain to nearly 3%, while shares also finished the week marginally higher. BofA called UnitedHealth’s quarter “impressive,” noting that earnings beat consensus by 31% and guidance rose 12%. The firm raised its price target to $512, implying over 20% upside, while reiterating a ‘Buy’ rating and citing a “strong” quarter and broad-based outlook increase. Morgan Stanley was even more bullish, lifting its target to $529, implying a 24% upside. The firm said the Q2 beat and higher 2026 targets “validate its disciplined strategy and establish a stronger base for future growth.” Truist, Oppenheimer and KeyBanc each moved to $500 targets, implying a 17% upside. Truist highlighted top- and bottom-line beats, a better Medical Care Ratio, and improving expectations for UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health. Oppenheimer said that the company “handily” topped expectations, while KeyBanc said results “topped bullish expectations” and argued UnitedHealth could hit $30 in earnings per share (EPS) sooner than anticipated. Goldman Sachs and UBS both raised their targets to $490, implying a 15% upside. Goldman cited a “material” earnings beat, stronger Optum Health profitability and a larger-than-expected guidance increase. UBS said UnitedHealth was “making good progress with more to go.” Meanwhile, RBC Capital raised its target to $478, implying a 12% upside. It remained positive on the earnings beat and guidance hike but flagged investor concern around persistent commercial medical-cost pressure. UnitedHealth posted adjusted EPS of $6.38, beating the $4.92 consensus and rising from $4.08 a year ago. Revenue of $112.03 billion also topped estimates, while the medical care ratio improved to 86.7% from 89.4%. Additionally, the company raised its 2026 adjusted EPS outlook to $19.50-$20 from more than $18.25, lifted UnitedHealthcare’s operating profit forecast to at least $12 billion, and increased Optum Health’s outlook to at least $2.2 billion. CEO Stephen Hemsley said UnitedHealth was “returning to form” as stronger performance disciplines took hold. He reaffirmed the company’s 13%-16% long-term earnings-growth target and doubled the 2026 buyback goal to at least $5 billion. Medicare Advantage drove the beat, with costs coming in below expectations. “Medicare delivered a strong second quarter,” UnitedHealthcare CEO Tim Noel said. Commercial plans remained the weak spot, with medical-cost trends above 11%. On the other hand, Optum said its tools added nearly 200,000 patient-facing hours, cut clinician cognitive burnout by 90%, and achieved a 96% first-pass approval rate for digital prior authorizations. SpaceX (SPCX) shares rose 1% overnight heading into Monday after CEO Elon Musk dismissed a report claiming that the rocket and satellite company had placed a $52 billion order with Foxconn for Nvidia-powered AI servers. SPCX stock fell 5% on Friday, extending its weekly decline to 15%. “This is fake news,” Musk said on X in response to a post summarizing the reported agreement. Taiwan’s Economic Daily said that Hon Hai Precision Industry, better known as Foxconn, had secured its first contract to manufacture AI servers for SpaceX. According to the report, SpaceX was preparing to deploy more than 13,000 server racks built around Nvidia’s GB300 platform. The estimated $52 billion value was based on an assumed cost of $4 million per rack rather than a disclosed contract price. Citrini analyst Jukan said on X that Foxconn had displaced the dominance of Dell Technologies and Super Micro Computer in supplying AI server infrastructure to SpaceX. It also claimed deliveries would begin in late 2026 and continue into the first quarter of 2027. Chairman Young Liu has previously said Foxconn expects to capture more than 40% of the global AI server market, while shipments of advanced AI racks are projected to increase through the end of the year. A separate Wall Street Journal report on Friday said that SpaceX was in discussions with the U.S. Department of Defense about supplying data-center capacity worth several billion dollars for military AI workloads. The talks were said to be ongoing and could still fail to produce an agreement. SpaceX has also explored offering computing power to outside AI customers as it seeks to compete more directly with cloud infrastructure providers such as CoreWeave. In June, SpaceX also reached computing arrangements with Google and Anthropic. The Google deal covered access to about 110,000 Nvidia chips, while Anthropic secured capacity at the company’s Colossus 1 data center in Memphis. The potential Defense Department arrangement would deepen SpaceX’s already extensive relationship with the U.S. military. The Pentagon relies on the company for rocket launches, satellite communications and missile-tracking systems. It is also seeking more computing capacity as intelligence agencies and military units increase their use of AI. SpaceX employees have reportedly discussed selling computing capacity at prices designed to compete with established cloud and specialized AI infrastructure providers. The Pentagon, meanwhile, is seeking funding for a new AI Arsenal initiative centered on access to high-end chips and computing resources. The military has also approved multiple tech companies, including SpaceX, Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Oracle, for classified AI-related work. ARK Investment Management founder-CEO Cathie Wood cheered Eli Lilly’s $3.8 billion AtaiBeckley acquisition on Sunday, calling it a “well-deserved” payoff for shareholders and a validation of Christian Angermayer’s psychedelic vision. ATAI stock rose 1% on Friday, adding 40% over the past five sessions and marking its best week in more than a year. Shares, however, were dipping more than 1% in overnight trading heading into Monday. Wood highlighted on X the biotech company’s role in bringing psychedelic medicines closer to mainstream clinical use: “Not only a well-deserved return for ATAI shareholders, this transaction validates Christian’s heartfelt mission and vision,” Wood said. She called Angermayer’s work with ATAI “one of the biggest catalysts of the psychedelic renaissance,” adding that clinical trials are increasingly validating the potential of psychedelics in treatment-resistant depression, post-traumatic stress disorder and broader mental health conditions. title: USNH launches free tuition program for New Hampshire families making up to $100K - WMUR
content: A college education could soon be more affordable for some Granite State families. Starting next fall, the University System of New Hampshire will cover tuition for eligible in-state students from families making up to $100,000 per year. "We wanted to launch this program called the New Hampshire Promise to cover the cost of tuition for New Hampshire residents who make up to $100,000," said Kim DeRego, UNH vice provost for enrollment management. The New Hampshire Promise program applies to full-time first-year students and qualifying transfers at the University of New Hampshire, Plymouth State University and Keene State College. Some current students said the program sounds like a good idea. "That would be nice," said UNH senior Pacy Morgado. "I mean, I'm in-state, so, obviously, it's the highest in-state tuition in the country, so that would be helpful." "It's pretty exciting news," said UNH sophomore Brynna Kurspahic. "I've had a couple of friends that haven't been able to come back to school because they can't afford it anymore." The program will eventually replace a current one called the Granite Guarantee, and students will remain tuition-free for as long as they're eligible. A New Hampshire resident attending UNH can expect to pay $16,304 per year in tuition. Then, between housing, food and other fees, they have another $19,452 in costs. That adds up to more than $35,000 per year. Students in the program can get additional financial help in other ways. "Families can qualify for lots of other types of aid, including government aid and loans and things like that and other grant programs that are available," DeRego said. Some current students said they're worried about what the program could mean for their tuition, but university officials said there will be no impact. "We are not lowering the scholarships for students in order to fund these," DeRego said. "We're really trying to make the campus experience affordable for all of our students." Students don't need to apply for the program. They will be automatically considered when they fill out their FAFSA. title: UNH, Keene, Plymouth offer free tuition to NH families earning up to $100K - seacoastonline.com
content: DURHAM — The University System of New Hampshire is rolling out a free tuition program in fall 2027 for all newly enrolled in-state students whose families earn a maximum of $100,000 annually. First-year students and transfer students who previously earned an associate degree through the state’s community college system are eligible for the program to be offered at the University of New Hampshire, Keene State College and Plymouth State University. The new USNH program, New Hampshire Promise, will launch ahead for the 2027-2028 academic year and replace the Granite Guarantee program, which currently offers free tuition to Pell grant-eligible in-state students. “New Hampshire’s public institutions of higher education are a transformative opportunity for students,” USNH Chancellor Cathy Provencher said in a prepared statement Oct. 1. “In launching this new program, all of the university system institutions are working together to make higher education more accessible for more New Hampshire students, enabling them to pursue their dreams right here in the Granite State.” The median household income in New Hampshire is just over $99,000, as last reported by the U.S. Census Bureau. Tania deLuzuriaga, a spokesperson for UNH, said the school projects 29% more incoming UNH students will be eligible for New Hampshire Promise than the existing Granite Guarantee program it is replacing. An average of 900 to 1,000 UNH students enroll via the Granite Guarantee program per year, according to deLuzuriaga. “When President (Elizabeth) Chilton got here a little over two years ago, she wanted to shift our need-based program into something income-based just so it was something more families could take advantage of,” she said. Students enrolling at UNH Manchester and for the university’s online courses will be eligible for the new program, too. The university system will not cap the number of students that can enroll in the New Hampshire Promise program. All admitted students meeting the income and education standards, in addition to a minimum 2.7 grade point average requirement, will be automatically accepted after filing their Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA). There is no separate application to enroll in New Hampshire Promise when the program takes effect. The free tuition will remain in effect should a future student enroll in another USNH institution, so long as they continue to meet the income and education guidelines. “Awards will be based on an annual review of a student’s FAFSA, academic status, and full-time student status,” USNH says. Created in 2017, the Granite Guarantee program will be phased out in several years. Over 4,000 in-state students within the university system have qualified for the program since its founding. Current Granite Guarantee students cannot join the New Hampshire Promise program, though they will retain their financial assistance for the remainder of their undergraduate studies. In-state tuition at UNH’s flagship Durham campus currently stands at $16,304 per year, excluding room and boarding costs. New Hampshire students pay $15,444 per year at Plymouth State University and $12,348 per year at Keene State College. Before the 2025-2026 school year, in-state tuition rates across the university system were unfrozen for the first time in six years. The tuition aid program announcement comes amid declining undergraduate enrollment at UNH’s Durham and Manchester campuses and in its online student population. Last semester, 11,948 full- and part-time undergraduate students attended UNH, down from 13,631 students in the fall 2016 semester, according to a university dashboard.

title: Giant pumpkins grow from Durham retirement community project with UNH - Granite Post News
content: Giant pumpkins in Durham, NH, are headed to the Deerfield Fair after a growing project brought together residents of Brookdale Spruce Wood, the University of New Hampshire, families, friends and neighbors. Giant pumpkins in Durham, NH, are headed to the Deerfield Fair after a growing project brought together residents of Brookdale Spruce Wood, the University of New Hampshire, families, friends and neighbors. Residents of the retirement community grew five massive pumpkins with help from UNH plant-breeding expert Christopher Hernandez. Several are approaching 800 pounds, and the largest reached about 1,000 pounds before splitting open. To keep reading—and get local New Hampshire news sent daily to your inbox—sign up for our free newsletter! Inspired by the image, Cross and fellow resident, friend and outdoor partner-in-crime Daniel Reich, 86, began researching how to grow a giant pumpkin of their own. Their efforts led them to Christopher Hernandez, assistant professor of plant breeding at the University of New Hampshire. With his guidance, Cross and Reich laid out and rototilled three pumpkin patches. They then made 10 trips to Coyote Spring Farm in Lee to haul horse manure back to the patches. With Hernandez’s help, they obtained seeds from two prize-winning pumpkins, including one grown in 2018 by Steve Geddes of Boscawen that weighed 2,528 pounds (a US record for six years). On June 5, Cross, Reich and Hernandez planted four pumpkin seedlings – initially grown by UNH students – in each of the three pumpkin patches surrounding Brookdale Spruce Wood. Geddes donated retired paper-mill conveyor-belt squares to serve as sturdy “beds” for the pumpkins. He and Hernandez also taught the team about support and cushioning, including the use of sand and pool noodles. Old sheets provided shade and protection from the sun. Cross and Reich tended the plants every day and with Hernandez’s guidance, the team narrowed the field to the two strongest plants in each patch and carefully assisted with pollination. Over the next 16 weeks, throughout July, August and September, the once-tiny seeds/seedlings grew rapidly. The project soon attracted attention beyond Brookdale Spruce Wood. Members of the New Hampshire Giant Pumpkin Association paid the community a visit. Neighbors from the surrounding community stopped by during their daily walks to check on the pumpkins, while visiting family and friends did the same. Those regular visits sparked conversations and new friendships. The largest pumpkin, affectionately named “Frankenstein,” reached an impressive 1,000 pounds before splitting open! Despite the major disappointment, the project continued. Brookdale Spruce Wood residents helped name the four remaining pumpkins: The winning pumpkin will be sent to the Deerfield Fair to compete on Thursday, Oct. 1 against approximately 30 other pumpkins in the heaviest giant-pumpkin and/or prettiest giant-pumpkin competition.
